articles.headline: OFAC Issues Amended Iran-Related General License FF-1 for Iraq Development Bank Wind-Down
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued Iran-related General License (GL) FF-1, which amends and supersedes GL FF. This new license extends the authorization for transactions necessary to wind down dealings involving the International Development Bank for Investment and Finance, also known as Iraq Development Bank, and any entities it directly or indirectly owns by 50 percent or more.

The wind-down period has been extended from October 30, 2026, to December 1, 2026. A key provision of the amended license requires that any payments made to a blocked person must be deposited into a blocked account.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.region: North Korea, Democratic Republic of the Congo
articles.headline: OFAC Designates Individuals and Entity for North Korean IT Worker Schemes; Sanctions Rwandan Entities for DRC Support
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new designations targeting North Korean government-run IT worker schemes. Ten individuals and one entity were sanctioned for their involvement in these schemes, which reportedly defraud U.S. businesses and generate revenue for North Korea's weapons programs.

Additionally, OFAC sanctioned the Rwandan Ministry of Defence and Zigama Credit and Savings Society, a Rwandan financial institution. These actions were taken due to their alleged facilitation of Rwanda's support for the March 23 Movement (M23) and its political wing in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. The Treasury stated that these measures aim to hold Rwanda accountable under the Washington Accords and pressure the country to cease its support for M23 and withdraw its forces from eastern DRC.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: Extreme Networks, Inc. Reaches $1.53 Million Settlement with OFAC for Russia Sanctions Violations
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced a settlement agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., resolving potential civil liability for nine apparent violations of Russia sanctions. The settlement amount is $1,529,685.

The violations involved the export of networking equipment and services to a blocked Russian defense manufacturer. OFAC determined that the apparent violations were voluntarily self-disclosed and egregious. Separately, the Department of Justice announced a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc., under which the company will pay $975,721.84 in criminal penalties. OFAC credited $487,861 of this payment against its settlement, leaving $1,041,824 owed to OFAC.
articles.source: U.S. Treasury OFAC / ABA Banking Journal

articles.headline: OFAC Amends Frequently Asked Questions on Blocking, Rejecting Transactions, and Reporting
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has issued amended Frequently Asked Questions (FAQs) regarding blocking and rejecting transactions and filing reports with OFAC. This update aims to provide further clarity and guidance to entities on their compliance obligations.

The amendments are part of OFAC's ongoing efforts to ensure that financial institutions and other regulated entities have the most current information to effectively implement sanctions programs and report relevant activities.

articles.headline: OFAC Announces Iran-Related Designations, Belarus and North Korea Removals, and New General Licenses
body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced new Iran-related designations. Concurrently, OFAC has removed certain designations related to Belarus and North Korea, indicating a recalibration of sanctions efforts in these regions.

In addition to the designations and removals, OFAC has issued new Iran-related and Russia-related General Licenses. These licenses are accompanied by amended Frequently Asked Questions, providing updated guidance for navigating transactions and compliance within these sanctions programs.

body: The Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) has announced designations under the Protecting American Intellectual Property Act of 2022 (PAIPA). These actions are aimed at safeguarding American intellectual property from theft and illicit acquisition.

In conjunction with these designations, OFAC has issued associated General Licenses to provide guidance and authorization for certain transactions that may otherwise be prohibited. This move underscores the U.S. government's commitment to protecting its technological and economic interests.

articles.headline: OFAC Implements Counter Narcotics and Counter Terrorism Designations

articles.headline: Bank of America, N.A. Settles with OFAC for $11,662,930
body: Bank of America, N.A. has reached a settlement with the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) for $11,662,930. This penalty is part of a coordinated action by the U.S. Treasury Department, which also included a $1.2 billion penalty from FinCEN and a $750 million civil money penalty from the OCC for anti-money laundering and sanctions failures.

The OFAC settlement resolves 475 apparent sanctions violations that occurred between September 18, 2021, and April 24, 2025, with a total transaction value of approximately $14.83 million. These violations spanned various sanctions programs, including Russia, Belarus, Iran, Burma, Somalia, narcotics, and global terrorism. The conduct included payments via blocked banks, flaws in alert prioritization, delays in watchlist updates, and account mishandling.

articles.headline: Iran Warns of 'New Battlefield' After Reported US Strike on Qeshm Island
body: Iran's parliament speaker, Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf, warned on Tuesday that any 'strategic error' by the United States would open 'a new battlefield in the war,' hours after a reported US Air Force jet strike on an IRGC missile system on Qeshm Island. Ghalibaf stated that Iran is at its highest level of defensive readiness and that responsibility for preventing further escalation rests with Washington.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian also commented on Tuesday, stating that a return to war would benefit 'no one,' following the reported US strikes on the Iranian island in the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC separately claimed that its electronic warfare systems had downed two US MQM-170 reconnaissance drones south of Qeshm Island and destroyed a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz.

Residents of Qeshm Island, Hengam, and Bandar Abbas reported successive explosions and tremors overnight. US media outlets, citing unnamed officials, reported that a US Air Force jet struck an IRGC surface-to-air missile launch system on Qeshm Island after a missile was fired from the island at a US aircraft in the Strait of Hormuz. The operation was described as limited and aimed at protecting commercial shipping.

articles.headline: North Korea Tests Strategic Cruise Missile with Cluster Warhead, Plans Military Deployment
body: North Korea test-fired strategic cruise missiles on Monday, equipped with a new cluster-munition warhead, according to the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA). The DPRK Missile Administration assessed the cluster warhead's power and verified the missile's flight characteristics during a vertical strike on a target.

KCNA reported that the medium-sized dispersal warhead is capable of devastating a target area of 5 to 6 hectares with its 'highest-density power.' The test also 'perfected the capability to deliver a vertical strike against the target by improving the terminal manoeuvrability of the cruise missile,' taking into account the natural and geographical characteristics of the targeted area.

This marks the second announcement of cluster warhead tests in recent days, following an October 31 test of a similar warhead for a tactical ballistic missile. Pyongyang has announced plans to equip military units with four categories of such munitions by the end of 2026.

articles.headline: US Urges Venezuela to Follow Phased Plan for Democratic Transition
body: The United States has urged Venezuela to continue on a phased plan of economic recovery and political reconciliation before democratic elections. Secretary of State Marco Rubio discussed this gradual plan with Venezuelan Minister of Foreign Affairs Oliver Blanco during a meeting on Monday.

The State Department reaffirmed President Donald Trump's 'three-phase plan for Venezuela: stabilization, economic recovery and political reconciliation, and democratic transition.' The two diplomats discussed progress in Venezuelan-led reconciliation talks, including institutional reforms to lay the groundwork for free, fair, and credible elections. Secretary Rubio also called for the continued release of political prisoners still held in Venezuela.

This meeting comes nearly a year after US forces abducted former Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro from Caracas to face drug trafficking and other charges in the US. Interim President Delcy Rodriguez has led Venezuela under Washington's oversight since Maduro's ouster in January.

articles.headline: BIS Streamlines Export Controls for Sound Suppressors, Transfers to Commerce Control List
body: The Department of Commerce's Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) has announced that, as of November 20, 2026, the export of certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors will be subject to BIS's Export Administration Regulations (EAR), rather than the State Department's U.S. Munitions List.

This deregulatory action aims to align export controls on suppressors with those already applied to firearms. Under the new rule, suppressors will be added to the Commerce Control List (CCL), and BIS will require a license for certain exports, reexports, or in-country transfers, including releases of related software and technology to foreign persons. License exceptions currently available for firearms will also be applicable to suppressors.

Jeffrey I. Kessler, Under Secretary of Commerce for Industry and Security, stated that this move is a 'common-sense action that alleviates the compliance burden on America's proud firearms industry, while continuing to protect national security.'

articles.headline: Streamlining Export Controls for Drone Exports
body: The Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is easing export controls on certain Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs or drones) and related parts, components, accessories, attachments, technology, and software under the Export Administration Regulations (EAR). Specifically, this rule: eliminates wind gust tolerance as a parameter for determining UAV controls under the EAR; increases the threshold for national security controls on certain UAVs from an endurance of 30 minutes to an endurance of 3 hours; makes conforming changes to remove national security controls on software and technology associated with UAVs with an endurance less than 3 hours; maintains military end-use and end-user controls on those lower endurance drones and associated software and technology; clarifies Commerce Control List (CCL) controls for certain UAVs specially designed for military use; and removes national security controls on certain specially designed parts, components, accessories, and attachments for such UAVs as they do not provide any significant military or intelligence capabilities.

articles.headline: Implementation of EAR Export Controls on Silencers, Mufflers, and Sound Suppressors; and Other Firearms Related Changes
body: The Department of Commerce (Commerce), Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) is revising the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) and the Commerce Control List (CCL) to appropriately control certain silencers, mufflers, and sound suppressors (sound suppressors) that will no longer be described on the International Traffic in Arms Regulations U.S. Munitions List (USML). This interim final rule (IFR) complements a Department of State interim final rule published elsewhere in this issue of the Federal Register (International Traffic in Arms Regulations: USML Category I Firearm Suppressors (1400-AG11) (State IFR)). This transfer of jurisdiction will reduce the regulatory burden on exports of sound suppressors. This IFR also revises the EAR to allow firearms and related items to be temporarily exported and reexported under a license exception as tools of trade, thereby relieving exporters of the regulatory burden of applying for authorization. Finally, this IFR clarifies which items fall within the scope of the EAR's entry clearance requirements for a temporary import.

articles.headline: Enhanced Favorable Treatment for the United Arab Emirates Under the Export Administration Regulations
body: In this final rule, the Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS) amends the Export Administration Regulations (EAR) to provide enhanced favorable treatment for the United Arab Emirates (UAE). Specifically, BIS is removing the UAE from Country Groups D:3 and D:4 and adding the UAE to Country Group A:5. More license exceptions will now be available, including Strategic Trade Authorization (STA) for the UAE Government and approved commercial entities in the UAE. STA will authorize the export, reexport, or transfer (in-country) of military items; certain commercial satellites and spacecraft; and dual-use items useful in, inter alia, oil and gas production, desalination, and civil nuclear power generation. The UAE Government and approved commercial entities will also have license-free access to advanced computing items, consistent with the May 2025 U.S.-UAE Artificial Intelligence Cooperation framework, without compromising U.S. digital infrastructure buildout.

articles.headline: OCC Imposes $750 Million Assessment Against Bank of America for Deficient BSA/AML Compliance
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a $750 million civil money penalty against Bank of America, N.A. (bank), for violations of the Bank Secrecy Act and its implementing regulations, including 12 CFR 21.21 and 12 CFR 21.11. This amount is the largest in OCC history.

articles.headline: OCC Assesses $350 Million Civil Money Penalty Against American Express
body: The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) today announced a cease-and-desist order and a $350 million civil money penalty against American Express National Bank, Sandy, Utah (bank), for deficiencies in the bank's Bank Secrecy Act (BSA) and anti-money laundering (AML) compliance program.
